summary.text: Alexander is remembered as a Valaam monk and founder in the Russian North. His received life includes a vision of the Trinity and the growth of a monastery around his forest cell.

blocks.text: The OCA names his peasant parents Stephen and Vassa and his baptismal name Amos. He leaves an arranged marriage for Valaam, spends years as a novice and receives tonsure as Alexander in 1474. His parents later also become monastics.

blocks.text: Goiko’s 2026 account describes the cave associated with him on Valaam’s Holy Island and a later skete dedicated to him. It follows his departure to the River Svir, where solitude gave way to visitors after the hunter Andrei Zavalishin found his hut. The same article presents his bodily labours alongside the monks after he became abbot. These episodes belong to the published monastic life; they do not supply a new ascetic regimen for the reader.

blocks.text: The OCA dates the departure from Valaam to 1485 and the hunter’s discovery to 1493. It places the vision of three radiant angelic visitors in 1508 and connects it with a Trinity church. Alexander subsequently accepts priesthood and leadership, while continuing ordinary work such as baking and gathering firewood.

blocks.text: The OCA gives August 30, 1533 and age85 for his repose, after instructions concerning burial. Goiko’s account gives age83. These are differing printed ages; the app does not infer a harmonized birthday from them. Neither account describes martyrdom.

blocks.text: The 1998 pilgrimage report offers a later first-person witness to the veneration of relics identified as Alexander’s. The writer describes learning of their rediscovery in a Saint Petersburg newspaper and visiting the church of Saint Sophia and her daughters, where they rested temporarily. A guardian monk opens the coffin; the pilgrim reports seeing preserved skin and myrrh. The account also recalls the Trinity vision through a quotation from The Northern Thebaid. This is a published personal testimony to a visit and reported miracles, not an independent scientific examination or a newly verified account of every relic’s movement. Its 1998 setting and Russian Church Abroad perspective remain explicit.

blocks.text: The pilgrim explicitly compares the inward response at the shrine with two earlier experiences: ordination in 1979 and John Maximovitch’s 1994 glorification. That comparison identifies the passage as personal religious testimony. The writer’s questions about the Moscow Patriarchate also locate the report within the divided Russian ecclesiastical circumstances of its time, rather than a timeless description of present church relations.
